Gun mount: the gun comes to your face

The gun mount is the movement that brings the gun up to your cheek and shoulder. Coaches teach “muzzles first”: your front hand starts the barrels moving along the target’s path. While they move, the stock comes up to your cheek and settles into the shoulder pocket, the soft hollow between the collarbone and the shoulder joint. “Move, mount, shoot” is one smooth movement, not three separate ones. Bring the gun to your face, not your face to the gun. Keep your cheek on the comb, the top edge of the stock. A shotgun has no rear sight: your eye does that job, so it must sit in the same place each time.

A good mount is the same each time. Your head stays level and still, and your cheek settles on the comb of the stock. If you drop or tilt your head to meet the stock, your eye lands in a different place on each shot. Mount faults and their cures are in Mount errors: late, face to the gun, canting.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ you start with the gun down. Before you call, the heel of the stock (the top corner of its rear end) touches your body. It stays below a line marked on your vest in a colour that stands out, 25 cm below the shoulder axis. You hold this position until the target is out and you can see it. Mount earlier and the referee gives a verbal warning with a yellow card. Do it again on the same layout and you get a red card. A single target is then scored zero; for a double, the rule sets the score of both targets (Chapter 12 · Red card on repeat at the same layout).

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 3 · Ready position: feet and gun

In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free, so the gun may already be shouldered. In both disciplines each target is shot with the gun at the shoulder, and in Sporting™ the gun position is free between the two targets of a double.

A British coach may say “gun up” or “pre-mount this one”. That is illegal in a FITASC Sporting™ competition, normal in Compak® Sporting, and only a drill in training. Mounting and swinging along an imagined line before calling (mock shooting) is forbidden in Sporting™: a warning first, then a zero.

Safety: Away from the stand, keep the gun open and do not swing it at imagined targets. In Compak® Sporting mounting and swinging is also not allowed while another squad member is shooting.

Tip: Gun fit matters too. A stock of the wrong length or comb height makes a repeatable mount hard; a coach or gun fitter can check it (Gun fit basics). Mount practice at home with a checked, unloaded gun is possible only where your country’s law allows it, and only as your coach shows you (Dry practice of the mount).

Key points

  • Muzzles first, gun to face, cheek on the comb: move, mount, shoot.
  • Sporting™: stock below the vest line (25 cm under the shoulder axis) until the target is visible.
  • Compak® Sporting: free gun position at the call; always shoot from the shoulder.
  • Sporting™: pre-mount only as a training drill; in Compak® Sporting the gun may be mounted at the call.
  • Check gun fit with a coach; practise at home only where the law allows it.

Did you know?

The vest line rule applies to any type of stock, including adjustable combs and Monte Carlo stocks (with a raised comb). What counts is the highest point at the rear of the stock.

Stand Talk

  • Coach Gun to your face, not your face to the gun.

    Meaning: Lift the stock to the cheek; do not drop the head to meet the gun.

  • Coach Muzzles first — move, mount, shoot.

    Meaning: Start the barrels moving with the target, mount during the move, fire as the mount is complete.

  • Coach Your mount's late and too fast — start it with the front hand.

    Meaning: The gun comes up too late and with a jerk; the front hand should lead the movement earlier.

  • Coach Low gun on this one, like in competition.

    Meaning: Start with the stock below the vest line, as the FITASC Sporting™ rules require.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. In Sporting™, until when must the stock stay below the vest line?

    1. Until the shooter has called
    2. Until the referee gives a nod
    3. Until the target is out and visible
    4. Until the first shot is fired
    Answer

    Until the target is out and visible

    The ready position is held until the target has been released and can be seen; only then may the gun be mounted.

    Chapter 3 · Ready position: feet and gun

  2. In Compak® Sporting, may a shooter call for the target with the gun already at the shoulder?

    1. No: it earns a yellow card
    2. Only for rabbits and other low targets
    3. Only between the two targets of a double
    4. Yes: the gun position at the call is free
    Answer

    Yes: the gun position at the call is free

    Compak® Sporting has no low-gun rule: the gun may be mounted or not at the call, but each target is shot from the shoulder.

    Chapter 17 · Gun position when calling

  3. Why do coaches insist on the cheek staying on the comb?

    1. The eye works as the rear sight, so it must sit in one place
    2. To reduce the noise reaching the ear
    3. Because the rules of both disciplines require it
    4. To hide the face from the referee
    Answer

    The eye works as the rear sight, so it must sit in one place

    A shotgun has no rear sight: your eye does that job, so a lifted cheek sends the shot high.
